newsitem.title: KENYA: Milling losses, charges hit Kenya coffee.
newsitem.headline: Milling losses, charges hit Kenya coffee.

text.p: High milling losses of as much as 24 percent and a steady rise in milling charges threaten Kenya's coffee sector, a report by a government agency said on Sunday.

It said that despite liberalisation of coffee milling, the resultant enhanced competition and better technologies had not eased milling losses or helped cut milling charges in one of Kenya's key farm industries.
A report on coffee milling by an agriculture ministry agency showed that milling charges had soared in the last three years, although inflation was falling and labour was cheap and easily accessible.

The report showed that the Kenya Planters' Cooperative Union (KPCU), until 1994 a virtual milling monopoly, charged farmers 1,400 shilling per tonne to mill coffee in 1991/92 (October/September) but raised the charges to 2,436 shillings in 1994/95 and 3,770 shillings in 1994/95 and 1995/96.

It said that Thika Coffee Mills, launched only two years ago, charged 3,480 shilling per tonne to mill coffee while Socfinaf, one of the other five millers licensed since 1994, charged the current KPCU rate of 3,770 shilling per tonne.

"This would appear to be a cartel-like operation. We would expect that with better technologies and more competition, charges would come down and farmers would earn a little more from their efforts," the report said. "This is an area that requires streamlining to encourage increased production."

Milling involves hulling and polishing of parchment coffee to produce clean (green) coffee. Hulling is the removal of parchment skin (endorcarp) while polishing is the removal of sliver skin (endosperm), according to Kenyan farm experts.
In the process of milling, the coffee beans are separated from the husks. The husks comprise the milling loss.
The husks are sold for firing boilers and as mulch. None of the Kenyan millers so far passes the proceeds of these sales to coffee farmers, the report said.

"Milling losses indicate the technical efficiency of coffee milling. Where losses are higher, farmers make a loss because they have to provide a larger volume of parchment for a given volume of clean coffee," the report said.
Coffee is ranked behind tourism and tea as Kenya's leading foreign exchange earner.
